sections.title: The field where India kept changing hands
sections.intro_md:
Drive 90 km north of Delhi on the old Grand Trunk Road and you cross the same flat wheat country where the fate of north India was settled again and again. At **Tarain** in 1192 Prithviraj Chauhan lost to Muhammad of Ghor and the Delhi Sultanate followed. At **Panipat** in 1526 Babur's guns ended the Lodis and began the Mughals. At Panipat again in 1556 a chance arrow in the eye of Hemu handed India to Akbar. At **Karnal** in 1739 Nadir Shah broke the Mughal army in three hours and walked off with the Peacock Throne. At Panipat a third time, in 1761, the Marathas lost a generation of men in a single day.

The reason is geography. Haryana is the narrow dry corridor between the Thar desert and the Himalayan foothills, the only easy road from the north-west into the Gangetic plain. Every army had to come through it.

Today the same corridor carries the NH-44 highway, a hydrogen train, and the commuters of Gurugram. This is the story of how a battlefield became one of India's richest states.

spotlights.name: The Third Battle of Panipat
spotlights.spot_it: A brick obelisk in a quiet garden, Kala Amb ('black mango'), a few km from Panipat town.
spotlights.story_md: On Makar Sankranti, 14 January 1761, a Maratha army under Sadashivrao Bhau met Ahmad Shah Abdali's Afghans here after a two-month standoff in which the Marathas, cut off from supplies, had begun to starve. More than 125,000 troops fought. Historians estimate 60,000 to 70,000 were killed in the fighting, and an eyewitness chronicle says about 40,000 Maratha prisoners were massacred the next day. Legend says a mango tree on the field turned black from the blood, hence the name. In Marathi, 'Panipat zhala' (a Panipat happened) still means a total disaster.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It broke Maratha power in the north and cleared the road for the British, who took Bengal's revenues four years later.
spotlights.memory_hook: A mango tree turned black, and a whole language got a word for catastrophe.

sections.title: Haryana at a glance
sections.intro_md:
Haryana is small: **44,212 km²**, about 1.3% of India, twentieth or twenty-first in size depending on how you count. It wraps around Delhi on three sides, so a third of the state sits inside the National Capital Region.

It was carved out of Punjab on **1 November 1966**, the Hindi-speaking south-east of the old province. It still shares its capital, **Chandigarh**, with Punjab, and Chandigarh itself belongs to neither: it is a Union Territory. Census 2011 counted **25,351,462** people; estimates put 2025 near 3.1 crore. Since 22 December 2025 there are **23 districts**, the newest being Hansi.

The numbers that matter are lopsided. Haryana has about 2% of India's people but produced close to 4% of national output in 2025-26. Its per capita GSDP, **₹4,41,216**, is about 1.75 times India's. It gives every Indian more than twice the national average of milk. And at birth, for most of the last 40 years, it has had fewer girls per boy than almost any state in India.

spotlights.name: The shared capital
spotlights.spot_it: Le Corbusier's raw concrete assembly with an upturned funnel roof, beside a reflecting pool.
spotlights.story_md: When Punjab was split in 1966, neither side would give up Chandigarh, the new city Nehru had commissioned from Le Corbusier. So both kept it. Haryana's 90-member assembly meets in one wing of the Palace of Assembly, Punjab's in another, and the city is run by the Centre as a Union Territory. Haryana has periodically planned a capital of its own and never built one. The Capitol Complex is part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing of Le Corbusier's works since 2016.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Few states in the world legislate from a city they do not own.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two states, one building, and a landlord in Delhi.

sections.title: The land: hills, a desert edge and a vanished river
sections.intro_md:
Haryana is mostly flat alluvial plain between two great rivers, the **Yamuna** on its eastern border and the seasonal **Ghaggar** in the west. Four other landscapes frame it.

In the north the **Shivalik** foothills rise to Haryana's highest point, **Karoh peak, 1,467 m**, in the Morni Hills. In the south-west the plain dries into the sand of the **Thar** around Sirsa, Bhiwani and Mahendragarh, where summer temperatures pass 45°C. In the south the worn stumps of the **Aravalli**, among the oldest mountains on Earth, run through Gurugram and Faridabad toward Delhi.

Forest is scarce: officially about 3.6% of the land, among the lowest in India. That makes the few wild places precious, and they include two Ramsar wetlands, Sultanpur and Bhindawas. Water decides almost everything here, which is why canals, a disputed canal and a river that may or may not have been the Saraswati come up again and again in Haryana's story.

spotlights.name: Morni Hills and Karoh peak
spotlights.spot_it: Pine-and-scrub ridges with two small lakes, Tikkar Taal, an hour from Chandigarh.
spotlights.story_md: Most of Haryana lies below 300 m. Then, in the far north of Panchkula district, the land climbs into the Shivaliks. Morni village sits at 1,267 m, and Karoh peak nearby reaches 1,467 m, the state's roof. On clear winter days you can see the snow of the Himalaya. Tradition says the area takes its name from a queen, Morni, who ruled here two thousand years ago. The two Tikkar Taal lakes, said to be linked under the hill, are the closest thing Haryana has to a hill station.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Proof that Haryana is not all plain.
spotlights.memory_hook: Haryana's roof is a queen's name and two lakes holding hands underground.

spotlights.name: The Aravalli and Mangar Bani
spotlights.spot_it: Low, rocky, thorn-scrub ridges rising out of farmland south of Delhi.
spotlights.story_md: The Aravalli are worn down to hills now, but they shield the plain from the Thar's sand. In Faridabad district, villagers of Mangar have protected a hill forest called **Mangar Bani** for centuries as a sacred grove: no cutting, no grazing. Archaeologists later found stone tools there going back about 100,000 years and cave paintings, the first found in the Aravalli. The ridge is also a leopard corridor running from Sariska to Delhi, threatened by mining and real estate on every side.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The last green wall between Delhi and the desert.
spotlights.memory_hook: A grove guarded by faith turned out to hold India's oldest toolmakers.

spotlights.name: Sultanpur National Park
spotlights.spot_it: A shallow jheel ringed by acacia and mud islands, packed with storks and ducks in winter.
spotlights.story_md: Sultanpur covers just 1.43 km², smaller than many golf courses, yet it is one of north India's best bird sites. From October to March, migrants arrive from Siberia, Central Asia and Europe: bar-headed geese, pintails, greater flamingos, and nesting painted storks on the islands. The ornithologist Peter Jackson pushed for its protection in the 1970s with support from Salim Ali. In 2021 it and Bhindawas in Jhajjar became Haryana's first Ramsar wetlands of international importance. It sits 15 km from the glass towers of Gurugram.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A wetland that survives inside one of India's fastest-growing cities.
spotlights.memory_hook: Siberian geese commute to Gurugram every winter.

spotlights.name: Kalesar National Park
spotlights.spot_it: Dense sal forest and dry stream beds in the Shivalik foothills by the Yamuna.
spotlights.story_md: Kalesar is Haryana's wildest corner: about 53 km² of national park plus a sanctuary of similar size, joined to Simbalbara in Himachal and Rajaji in Uttarakhand. Leopards live here, and wild elephants walk in from Rajaji along the corridor. Tigers were long thought gone from Haryana, then in 2019 a camera trap caught one in Kalesar, the first record in the state in about a century. Sal trees dominate, close to the western edge of their range.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Haryana's only real forest and a link in the Himalayan elephant corridor.
spotlights.memory_hook: A tiger photographed in Haryana for the first time in a century.

spotlights.name: The Ghaggar, or the lost Saraswati?
spotlights.spot_it: A broad stony bed near Panchkula that carries water mainly in the monsoon.
spotlights.story_md: The Ghaggar rises in the Shivaliks, flows through Haryana and dies in the sands of Rajasthan. Across the border in Pakistan it is called the Hakra. Along its dry course lie hundreds of Harappan sites, including Rakhigarhi and Bhirrana, which suggests a much larger river once watered them. Many scholars and the Haryana government identify this system with the **Saraswati** of the Rigveda, and the state has a board working to revive it. Others say the river was mostly fed by monsoon rain, not glaciers, by Harappan times. The identification is still argued.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Haryana's ancient past is strung along this weak river.
spotlights.memory_hook: A river that fades into sand may be the goddess of learning.

sections.title: Deep history: Harappans, the Gita and a pillar that moved
sections.intro_md:
Haryana's past is older than its fields suggest. Along the Ghaggar lie some of the earliest and largest Harappan settlements: **Rakhigarhi**, **Bhirrana**, Banawali, Kunal. Charcoal from Bhirrana's lowest layers has been dated to the 8th to 7th millennium BCE, though how to read those dates is disputed.

Later, this was the land of the Kurus, one of the great kingdoms of the Vedic age. **Kurukshetra**, 'the field of the Kurus', is where the Mahabharata war is set and where Hindu tradition places the Bhagavad Gita. A circuit of 48 kos (about 150 km) around it holds hundreds of sacred tanks.

In the 7th century CE **Thanesar** was the home of Harsha, the last emperor to unite most of north India before the medieval kingdoms. Merchant towns like **Agroha** grew rich on the trade road to the north-west, the road that would later carry invaders and, in turn, give Haryana its battlefields.

spotlights.name: Rakhigarhi
spotlights.spot_it: Low mounds in wheat fields beside a village, with fenced excavation trenches.
spotlights.story_md: Rakhigarhi was one of the five largest Harappan cities. After two more mounds were found in 2014, the Archaeological Survey of India claimed it as the largest of all, at 300 to 350 hectares, though not all of that was one city at one time. In 2019 a team including geneticist David Reich sequenced DNA from a woman buried here about 4,600 years ago. Of 61 skeletons tested, hers was the only one that yielded usable DNA. She had ancestry related to ancient Iranians and South Asian hunter-gatherers, and none from the Central Asian steppe.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The best window yet onto who the Harappans were.
spotlights.memory_hook: One woman's teeth, out of 61 skeletons, rewrote the ancestry debate.

spotlights.name: Jyotisar
spotlights.when: Identified by tradition with Adi Shankara, 8th century
spotlights.spot_it: An old banyan on a platform beside a tank, with a marble chariot of Krishna and Arjuna.
spotlights.story_md: Hindu tradition holds that here, before the Kurukshetra war, Krishna spoke the Bhagavad Gita to the hesitant Arjuna. The banyan on the spot is revered as an offshoot of the tree that witnessed it. Tradition credits Adi Shankara with identifying the site in the 8th century. Every evening there is a light-and-sound show, and the state markets Kurukshetra as part of a Krishna circuit with Mathura and Dwarka. Whether any war was fought here is a matter of faith; that the place has been sacred for well over a thousand years is not.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The physical anchor of the most widely read Hindu text.
spotlights.memory_hook: A tree's grandchild stands where Krishna is said to have spoken.

spotlights.name: Harsha of Thanesar
spotlights.spot_it: A brick mound in Thanesar town, and silver coins showing a king's head with a crescent.
spotlights.story_md: Harsha became king of Thanesar at 16 after his father died and his elder brother was murdered. He built an empire across north India and moved the capital to Kannauj, but his story begins here. The court poet Banabhatta's *Harshacharita* describes Thanesar's walls, moat and white palace. The Chinese pilgrim **Xuanzang** visited and praised Harsha's justice and charity, including a gift-giving festival every five years where he gave away his treasury. His southern advance was stopped at the Narmada by Pulakeshin II.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The last great north Indian emperor before the medieval age, and he was from Haryana.
spotlights.memory_hook: A teenage king from Thanesar who gave away his treasury every five years.

spotlights.name: The Topra pillar
spotlights.spot_it: A 13 m polished sandstone shaft on top of a ruined palace at Firoz Shah Kotla, Delhi.
spotlights.story_md: Emperor Ashoka raised this pillar at Topra, near Yamunanagar, carved with his edicts. In 1356 Sultan Firoz Shah Tughlaq, who loved old monuments, had it wrapped in cotton and silk, laid on a 42-wheeled cart pulled by hundreds of men, floated down the Yamuna on boats, and erected on his new palace in Delhi. Nobody could then read the script. In 1837 James Prinsep cracked Brahmi using inscriptions like this one, unlocking Ashoka for the modern world. Topra now has a replica.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Its text helped decipher Brahmi, the parent of most Indian scripts.
spotlights.memory_hook: A pillar wrapped in silk took a boat ride to Delhi.

spotlights.name: Agroha
spotlights.spot_it: An excavated brick mound called Ther beside a large modern temple complex on NH-9.
spotlights.story_md: The Agrawal and Agrahari communities trace their origin to Agroha and its legendary king, **Maharaja Agrasen**. The story says that when a new family came to settle, each of the city's households gave it one brick and one coin, so every newcomer arrived with a house and capital. Excavations on the mound have found coins, seals and sculpture from early centuries CE. Agroha Dham, a large temple built by the community, now draws pilgrims, and Hisar's new airport is named after Agrasen.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Some of India's great merchant families trace their ancestry to this mound.
spotlights.memory_hook: One brick and one coin from every house.

sections.title: Sultans, Mughals and rebels
sections.intro_md:
For most of the last thousand years Haryana was not a kingdom but a hinterland: the grain store and highway of whoever held Delhi. That made it rich in roadside monuments and poor in palaces.

The Delhi Sultans founded towns here. **Firoz Shah Tughlaq** built Hisar in 1354 and dug canals from the Yamuna to water it. **Sher Shah Suri** and the Mughals lined the Grand Trunk Road with kos minars and sarais. Sufis settled: the tomb of Sheikh Chilli at Thanesar is the finest Mughal building in the state.

Two figures from Haryana challenged the centre. **Hemu**, a trader-turned-general from Rewari, briefly took Delhi in 1556. **Banda Singh Bahadur** set up the first Sikh state at Lohgarh in 1710. In 1857 the region rose against the British: Rao Tula Ram of Rewari fought them at Nasibpur, and Haryana's villages paid for the revolt with confiscations and hangings.

spotlights.name: First Battle of Panipat
spotlights.spot_it: A Baburnama painting: cannon behind lashed carts, horsemen wheeling round the flanks.
spotlights.story_md: Babur came down from Kabul with a small army, perhaps 12,000 to 15,000 men, against Sultan Ibrahim Lodi's much larger force and war elephants. He chained carts together as a barricade, put field guns and matchlock men behind them, and sent cavalry round both flanks. The guns panicked the elephants. Ibrahim died on the field by noon, and his modest tomb still stands in Panipat. It was one of the first battles in India decided by gunpowder, and it founded the Mughal empire.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The day gunpowder changed Indian warfare.
spotlights.memory_hook: Carts, cannon and frightened elephants: the Mughal empire began before lunch.

spotlights.name: Hemu, the last Hindu king of Delhi
spotlights.spot_it: Mughal paintings show a man slumped on an elephant, an arrow in his eye.
spotlights.story_md: Hemu began, by most accounts, as a merchant supplying saltpetre in Rewari. He rose to be chief minister and general of the Sur sultan Adil Shah and won 22 battles against Afghan rebels and Mughals. In October 1556 he took Delhi and crowned himself **Vikramaditya**. A month later, at Panipat, he was winning against the teenage Akbar's army when an arrow struck his eye. His leaderless troops broke. He was captured unconscious and beheaded. Had the arrow missed, Indian history might have no Akbar.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The closest the Mughals came to being a footnote.
spotlights.memory_hook: One arrow, one eye, and Akbar's reign began.

spotlights.name: Sheikh Chilli's tomb
spotlights.spot_it: A white marble pear-shaped dome on a sandstone terrace, above a garden and a madrasa.
spotlights.story_md: This is Haryana's finest Mughal monument, sometimes called its Taj Mahal. It is the tomb of a Sufi saint, Abd-ur-Rahim, known as Sheikh Chehli, traditionally said to have been a teacher of Dara Shikoh, Shah Jahan's scholarly son. The marble dome and lattice screens echo Agra. Do not confuse him with the Sheikh Chilli of folk tales, the daydreamer who builds castles in the air and saws off the branch he sits on. The two share a name and, over time, a reputation in local jokes.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Mughal refinement in a town better known for the Mahabharata.
spotlights.memory_hook: A saint's tomb that shares a name with India's most famous daydreamer.

spotlights.name: Lohgarh, first Sikh capital
spotlights.spot_it: Stone ruins on wooded Shivalik slopes, now a memorial park with a statue of Banda Singh Bahadur.
spotlights.story_md: After Guru Gobind Singh's death, Banda Singh Bahadur led a peasant army across Punjab and Haryana. In 1710 he made Lohgarh, the 'iron fort' hidden in the Shivalik forest, the capital of the first Sikh state. He struck coins in the names of the Gurus, issued orders under a Khalsa seal and broke up big landholdings in favour of tillers. A Mughal army took the fort in 1710 and he escaped; in 1716 he was captured and executed in Delhi. Haryana is now developing the site.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The first time Sikhs ruled territory, and it was in Haryana.
spotlights.memory_hook: An iron fort hidden in the forest minted coins in the Gurus' names.

sections.title: How Haryana became Haryana
sections.intro_md:
For a century after 1858 the British treated this area as the poor south-eastern corner of Punjab, punished for 1857 and left short of canals. The man who changed its politics was **Sir Chhotu Ram** (1881 to 1945), a Jat lawyer from Rohtak whose laws freed peasants from moneylenders.

After independence, the Punjabi Suba movement wanted a Punjabi-speaking state. The **Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1966** gave it one and turned the Hindi-speaking districts into **Haryana**, born on 1 November 1966.

The early years were wild. In 1967 MLA Gaya Lal changed parties three times in two weeks, giving India the phrase **'Aaya Ram, Gaya Ram'** for turncoats and leading, eventually, to the anti-defection law of 1985. Three 'Lals' then dominated for 30 years: Bansi Lal, the road builder; Bhajan Lal; and Devi Lal, the farmers' 'Tau'. The unfinished business of 1966, water and the capital, still shapes the state.

spotlights.name: Sir Chhotu Ram
spotlights.spot_it: Look for the bespectacled man in a turban on a 1995 stamp and a 64 ft statue at Garhi Sampla.
spotlights.story_md: Born Ram Richpal in a Rohtak village, Chhotu Ram became the leading minister of undivided Punjab's Unionist government, an alliance of Hindu, Muslim and Sikh farmers. His 'golden laws' of the late 1930s let peasants recover land mortgaged to moneylenders and set up regulated grain markets, the mandis that still run north Indian farming. Farmers called him 'Deenbandhu', friend of the poor. He is also credited with pushing the Bhakra dam project. Farm unions still invoke his name at every agitation.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He built the mandi system that Punjab and Haryana farmers defended in 2020-21.
spotlights.memory_hook: The farmers' messiah who made the moneylender give the land back.

spotlights.name: Devi Lal, 'Tau'
spotlights.spot_it: A heavy man in a white kurta and turban, statues of whom stand in most Haryana towns.
spotlights.story_md: Devi Lal fought for a separate Haryana, then twice became its chief minister (1977 to 1979 and 1987 to 1989) and was India's Deputy Prime Minister from 1989 to 1991. He was called **Tau**, elder uncle. His 1987 government introduced a monthly old-age pension for rural elderly, one of the first state pensions of its kind, which became a template for others. His family founded the Indian National Lok Dal, and his grandsons and great-grandsons still lead rival parties.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He made rural welfare a vote-winner in north India.
spotlights.memory_hook: Uncle of the whole state, pension in hand.

spotlights.name: The Sutlej Yamuna Link canal
spotlights.spot_it: A dry, weed-filled concrete channel that suddenly ends.
spotlights.story_md: When Haryana was carved out, it was promised a share of Punjab's river water through a 214 km canal linking the Sutlej to the Yamuna. Haryana finished its 92 km part. Punjab began its share, then stopped after violence in the 1980s, and in 2004 passed a law cancelling the water agreements. The Supreme Court struck that law down in 2016 and has repeatedly ordered completion. The canal is still not built in Punjab. Few infrastructure projects in India have been fought over so long.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Water, not language, is now the deepest Punjab-Haryana dispute.
spotlights.memory_hook: Half a canal, fifty years of lawsuits.

sections.title: Languages: Haryanvi, Hindi and Punjabi
sections.intro_md:
Haryana's official language is **Hindi**, and since 2010 **Punjabi** is the second official language. What people actually speak at home is mostly **Haryanvi**, a western Hindi language close to the Khari Boli of Delhi and the Braj of Mathura.

The census struggles with this. In 2011 about 48% of people reported Hindi as their mother tongue and 37% reported Haryanvi, though many who reported Hindi speak Haryanvi at home. Punjabi was 7.4%, mostly in the north and in towns settled by Partition refugees. Smaller languages include Bagri in the south-west near Rajasthan, Mewati in Nuh district, and Ahirwati around Rewari.

Haryanvi has a reputation, mostly affectionate, for being blunt. It drops the polite plural (people often say 'tu' where Hindi speakers say 'aap'), loves rhyme and insult, and has become the voice of a booming music industry on YouTube. Its sound is strong, with doubled consonants and a falling tone: 'ke haal se?' (how are you?).

spotlights.name: Haryanvi
spotlights.spot_it: Listen for 'se' for 'hai' ('ke haal se?'), 'thara' for 'your', and 'mhara' for 'our'.
spotlights.story_md: Haryanvi is not a 'rough Hindi' but a language with its own grammar and huge oral literature: saang plays, ragini songs, proverbs and riddles. Its standard greeting is 'Ram Ram'. Its pronouns are distinct ('mhara' our, 'thara' your), and 'se' does the work of Hindi 'hai'. A variety called Rangri, spoken by Muslim Ranghars, crossed into Pakistan in 1947 and survives there in Nastaliq script while it has vanished in Haryana. Today Haryanvi pop songs regularly pass a billion views online, carrying the dialect far beyond the state.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A language most of its speakers write down as 'Hindi'.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ke haal se? Mhara Haryana.

sections.title: Faith: Kurukshetra, goddesses and the Sikh trail
sections.intro_md:
Census 2011 counted **87.5% Hindus**, 7.0% Muslims and 4.9% Sikhs. Muslims are concentrated in **Nuh** (Mewat) district, home of the Meo community, where they are a large majority. Sikhs live mostly in the north and in towns settled after 1947.

The great Hindu centre is **Kurukshetra**, whose tanks draw lakhs of bathers during solar eclipses. Pilgrims also come to settle the dead: at Pehowa and Kurukshetra, family priests keep genealogy registers going back generations. Goddess shrines dot the foothills, the best known being **Mansa Devi** in Panchkula, which gave the town its name. Popular village faith centres on local saints and snake gods like **Gugga Pir**, worshipped by Hindus and Muslims alike.

The Sikh Gurus passed through repeatedly. Guru Gobind Singh stayed at Kapal Mochan and at Nada Sahib, and Guru Tegh Bahadur halted at several Haryana villages on his way to execution in Delhi in 1675.

spotlights.name: Brahma Sarovar
spotlights.when: Ancient; ghats rebuilt in the 20th century
spotlights.spot_it: A vast rectangular tank lined with steps and red sandstone pavilions, a temple on an island.
spotlights.story_md: Brahma Sarovar is about 1,100 m long and 450 m wide, one of the largest temple tanks in India. The story is that Brahma created the universe from here. During a solar eclipse, hundreds of thousands of people bathe at once, believing it equals the merit of a thousand horse sacrifices. In December the tank hosts the **International Gita Mahotsav**, with lamps floated at dusk. Family priests here keep registers of visiting families, recording births, deaths and pilgrimages over centuries.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Kurukshetra's main stage for ritual, festival and genealogy.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bathe during an eclipse, earn a thousand horse sacrifices.

spotlights.name: Mansa Devi, Panchkula
spotlights.spot_it: A temple complex on a Shivalik spur above Panchkula, crowded during the two Navratris.
spotlights.story_md: Mansa Devi is the goddess who fulfils wishes (mansa means wish). The main temple was built in the early 19th century by the ruler of Mani Majra, Gopal Singh, and a second temple in the complex was built by the Maharaja of Patiala in 1840. Since 1991 a shrine board run by the Haryana government manages it. During the spring and autumn Navratri fairs, lakhs of devotees climb up, and the city of Panchkula, which grew around it, is often called the land of Mansa Devi.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The goddess who gave her name to a whole planned city.
spotlights.memory_hook: Make a wish at Mansa, and Panchkula grew up around it.

spotlights.name: Pehowa (Prithudak)
spotlights.spot_it: A narrow channel of the old Saraswati with temples and priests seated at small desks.
spotlights.story_md: Pehowa, the old Prithudak, sits on the dried Saraswati bed. Hindus and Sikhs come here to perform pind daan, the rites for ancestors, especially for those who died untimely. The priests, called pandas, each hold registers for particular clans and villages, some going back several centuries. A visitor gives his family name and village, and the panda turns pages to show the signatures of grandfathers and great-grandfathers who came before. It is one of north India's living family archives.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Genealogy kept by hand, family by family, for centuries.
spotlights.memory_hook: Say your village, and a priest shows your great-grandfather's signature.

spotlights.name: Kapal Mochan
spotlights.spot_it: Three sacred tanks surrounded by temples and a gurdwara, busiest at the Kartik full moon.
spotlights.story_md: Hindu legend says bathing here frees one from the worst sin, killing a Brahmin; Shiva himself is said to have been cleansed here. The site is shared: Guru Nanak and Guru Gobind Singh both visited, and a hukamnama (an edict) records Guru Gobind Singh's stay in 1679. Each November at Kartik Purnima a large fair draws Hindus and Sikhs to bathe together. Nearby Adi Badri is where many believe the Saraswati leaves the hills.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A tirtha where Hindu and Sikh pilgrimage overlap.
spotlights.memory_hook: The pool that washes away even a god's sin.

sections.title: Saang, ragini and the voice of Hisar
sections.intro_md:
Haryana's classic performing art is not a court dance but village theatre. **Saang** (or swang, 'imitation') is open-air musical drama in which a troupe of ten or twelve tells a story from myth or folklore through song, dialogue and jokes, all night, on a platform surrounded by the audience. Men played the women's roles. The great name is **Pandit Lakhmi Chand**, whose plays and songs are still sung.

Out of saang grew **ragini**, sung verse duels in which two singers answer each other, accompanied by harmonium, dholak and sarangi. Ragini competitions still pack village grounds.

Dance is mostly seasonal and collective: **Phag** after the spring harvest, **Loor** by girls in Phalgun, **Ghoomar** and **Khoria** by women at weddings, the latter while men are away with the bridegroom's party. And from a village in Hisar came one of the great classical voices of the 20th century.

spotlights.name: Saang
spotlights.spot_it: A night-long show on an open platform: harmonium, dholak, a man in a woman's dress, and a crowd sitting on the ground all around.
spotlights.story_md: Saang is talk-heavy theatre: stories like Raja Harishchandra, Sorath or Dhruv Bhagat are told in rhymed verse with comic interruptions. Tradition credits Kishan Lal Bhaat with the modern form about two centuries ago. Before radio and TV, a saang troupe arriving in a village was the event of the season, and its songs became the region's popular music. Women were barred from the stage, so men played heroines, and audiences judged them on how well they did it. The form declined with cinema and now survives through festivals and YouTube.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The root of Haryanvi song, theatre and humour.
spotlights.memory_hook: All-night theatre where the heroine has a moustache under the veil.

spotlights.name: Pandit Lakhmi Chand
spotlights.spot_it: His name is on Haryana's state awards, a university of performing arts in Rohtak and countless ragini albums.
spotlights.story_md: Lakhmi Chand had no formal schooling. He grazed cattle as a boy, learned by ear, joined saang troupes and became the greatest poet the form produced, called the 'Kalidas of Haryana'. His plays mixed epic, romance and blunt moral comment, and his ragini lines on time, greed and fate are still quoted in village arguments. He died at about 42. In 2022 the film *Dada Lakhmi* told his story and won the National Film Award for best Haryanvi film.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Haryana's national poet, though he never wrote for print.
spotlights.memory_hook: A cowherd who became the Kalidas of Haryana.

spotlights.name: Phag, Loor and Ghoomar
spotlights.spot_it: Women in ankle-length daman skirts and heavy odhnis, moving in circles, clapping and turning to a dhol.
spotlights.story_md: Haryanvi dances are tied to the farm year. **Phag** is danced in Phalgun (February-March), when the wheat is green and there is time to celebrate; men and women tease each other in song. **Loor** is performed by girls in the Bangar region with question-and-answer lyrics. **Ghoomar** in southern Haryana shares its name and swirl with Rajasthan's. These forms are performed today by college troupes at youth festivals and in competitions like Kurukshetra University's Ratnawali.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Dances that mark the calendar of the wheat crop.
spotlights.memory_hook: When the wheat is green, Haryana dances.

spotlights.name: Pandit Jasraj
spotlights.spot_it: A silver-haired singer in a bright kurta, eyes closed, hand raised, singing 'Om Namo Bhagavate Vasudevaya'.
spotlights.story_md: Jasraj was born in a village near Hisar in 1930 and started as a tabla player before turning to voice at 14. He became the leading singer of the **Mewati gharana**, named after the Mewat region on Haryana's southern edge, and created the jasrangi style in which a man and a woman sing two different ragas at once. His career ran 75 years. In 2019 the International Astronomical Union named minor planet 300128 Panditjasraj after him.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A Hisar village boy who became one of India's great classical voices.
spotlights.memory_hook: There is an asteroid named after a singer from Hisar.

sections.title: Crafts and clothes: wall goddesses, embroidery, the daman
sections.intro_md:
Haryana's crafts are domestic rather than courtly: things women made for the home, the wedding and the festival.

In Navratri, women build **Sanjhi**, a goddess made of small clay or dung pieces pressed onto the courtyard wall. **Phulkari**, the darning-stitch embroidery shared with Punjab, decorated odhnis and wedding shawls; Haryana's version tends to be sparser, with motifs of animals and village life on a dark ground. Potters, weavers of durries and makers of the tall brass-and-clay hookah supplied every village.

The look of rural Haryana is the **daman**, a heavily pleated ankle-length skirt, worn with a kurti and a large odhni or chunder, and for men the dhoti, kurta and turban (pagri). Women's jewellery is silver and heavy: hansli neck rings, bangles, anklets. Much of this is now festival wear, but in villages it is still daily dress for older women.

spotlights.name: Sanjhi
spotlights.spot_it: A goddess face and body built of small clay stars, moons and discs on a mud wall, eyes of shells.
spotlights.story_md: On the first day of autumn Navratri, girls and women make a figure of the goddess Sanjhi on the wall from small dried clay or cow-dung shapes: stars, suns, moons, jewellery. Each evening they sing to her and offer food. On the tenth day, Dussehra, the figure is taken down and the pieces immersed in a pond. Sanjhi is linked to the coming of a new bride and to her brother's visit to bring her home. It is women's art, made fresh every year and destroyed every year.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Ephemeral art that keeps a folk goddess alive.
spotlights.memory_hook: A goddess built of clay stars for ten nights, then returned to the pond.

spotlights.name: Phulkari and bagh
spotlights.spot_it: Floss-silk darning stitches in gold and orange on coarse handspun cotton, worked from the back.
spotlights.story_md: Phulkari means 'flower work'. The embroiderer works from the reverse of khaddar cloth with untwisted silk, counting threads, so the pattern appears as shining geometric blocks. When the whole cloth is covered, it is called a **bagh** (garden). Grandmothers began a bagh at a girl's birth to give at her wedding. Haryana's phulkari tends to leave more ground visible and adds figures of animals and people. Much of it now sits in museums, and machine copies flood markets.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A dowry textile that recorded a family's patience.
spotlights.memory_hook: A garden stitched from the back for a girl not yet married.

spotlights.name: The daman
spotlights.spot_it: An ankle-length skirt with dozens of pleats, often 20 m of cloth, swinging as the wearer turns.
spotlights.story_md: The daman is a gathered skirt, sometimes using over 20 metres of cloth, usually in strong colours with borders. With it go a kurti or angi (blouse) and a large odhni pulled over the head and often over the face in front of elders, the custom of ghunghat. The phrase '52 gaj ka daman' (a skirt of 52 yards) became the title of a 2020 Haryanvi song by Renuka Panwar that passed a billion views on YouTube, turning village dress into pop iconography.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Dress as identity, and now as a viral song.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fifty-two yards of skirt and a billion views.

sections.title: Food: milk, millet and a 250 gram jalebi
sections.intro_md:
A Haryanvi saying sums up the diet: **'Desaan mein des Haryana, jit doodh dahi ka khana'**, the best land is Haryana, where milk and curd are the food. The numbers agree. In 2023-24 Haryana had **1,105 g of milk per person per day**, more than double the national 471 g and behind only Punjab and Rajasthan.

The cooking is plain, rural and built around grain and dairy. Winter means **bajra** (pearl millet) rotis with white butter, bajra khichdi, and greens like bathua and sarson. Summer means wheat rotis, lassi in brass tumblers, kadhi, and desert vegetables from the south-west: **kachri** (wild melon), singri beans, ker berries. Ghee goes on almost everything; churma, crushed roti with ghee and jaggery, is a treat.

On the highways, the food is famous: Murthal's paratha dhabas, Gohana's giant jalebis, Rewari's revdi, Hansi's peda.

spotlights.name: Bajra roti with white butter
spotlights.spot_it: A thick grey-green flatbread, rough-edged and hand-patted, with a lump of white butter melting on top.
spotlights.story_md: Pearl millet grows where wheat struggles, on the sandy soils of Bhiwani, Mahendragarh and Sirsa. Its flour has no gluten, so the roti cannot be rolled; it is patted between wet palms and baked on a griddle, then over open flame. In winter it is eaten with white butter, jaggery and saag, and leftover rotis are crumbled into churma. Bajra khichdi, cooked with moong dal and eaten with ghee and lassi, is a cold-night dinner. India is the world's largest grower of pearl millet.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A desert grain that fed Haryana long before the Green Revolution.
spotlights.memory_hook: Patted, not rolled: a roti that cannot hold together without your hands.

spotlights.name: Kadhi pakora
spotlights.spot_it: A pale yellow, sour yogurt curry with soft gram-flour fritters soaking in it.
spotlights.story_md: Kadhi uses what a dairy state has too much of: sour curd. It is whisked with gram flour, simmered slowly with turmeric, then tempered with cumin, fenugreek and dried red chilli. Pakoras of gram flour and onion go in to soak. Haryanvi kadhi is thinner and tangier than the Gujarati kind, which is sweet. It is eaten with rice or roti, and every family claims its own sourness. Leftover sour buttermilk is never wasted.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The everyday dish of the curd economy.
spotlights.memory_hook: If the curd is too sour to eat, make kadhi.

spotlights.name: Murthal paratha dhabas
spotlights.when: Highway food since the decades after Partition
spotlights.spot_it: A neon strip of huge dhabas on the Delhi-Chandigarh highway, open all night, with paratha stacked under slabs of white butter.
spotlights.story_md: Murthal is a village 45 km from Delhi on the GT Road. Truckers and travellers started stopping at its dhabas in the decades after Partition. Now a strip of enormous eateries serves stuffed parathas (potato, paneer, onion, mixed) with a fist-sized lump of white butter, curd and pickle, round the clock. A Delhi tradition is to drive out after midnight just to eat here. Most of the big dhabas are vegetarian, and on weekend nights the queues spill into the car parks.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The most famous food stop on India's busiest highway.
spotlights.memory_hook: Drive 45 km at midnight for a paratha.

spotlights.name: Gohana jalebi
spotlights.spot_it: A jalebi the size of a fist, thick-coiled, fried in desi ghee, about 250 grams each.
spotlights.story_md: Ordinary jalebis are thin and crisp. At Gohana, the shop of Lala Matu Ram fries them fat, in pure ghee, so that one piece weighs about a quarter kilo and is sold by the kilo. They are crisp outside and chewy inside, less sweet than they look, and keep for days, which is why travellers buy boxes to carry home. Rival shops all claim to be the 'original Matu Ram'. It became a talking point in the 2024 assembly election campaign.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A town known across India for one sweet.
spotlights.memory_hook: Four jalebis make a kilo in Gohana.

spotlights.name: Murrah buffalo
spotlights.spot_it: Jet black, glossy, with short horns that curl tightly into rings, and a huge udder.
spotlights.story_md: Murrah is the highest-yielding buffalo in India, and Haryana is its home: the official breeding tract is Rohtak, Hisar, Jind, Jhajjar, Bhiwani and nearby. Good cows give 15 to 20 litres a day; a record Murrah gave 26.3 kg in a day in 2016. The breed has been exported to Italy, Bulgaria, Egypt, Brazil and the Philippines to improve local herds. Prize bulls are celebrities at Haryana cattle fairs, with owners claiming crore-rupee valuations for them on the strength of semen sales.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The black gold behind Haryana's milk surplus.
spotlights.memory_hook: Curled horns, black coat, crore-rupee bulls.

compare.difference: Hariana is a white humped cow bred for both draught and milk; Murrah is a black buffalo bred for milk alone.

sections.title: Festivals and fairs
sections.intro_md:
Haryana's calendar follows the farm year and the Hindu lunar year. **Teej** in Sawan (July-August) welcomes the monsoon with swings and songs; the state treats it as a public holiday. **Gugga Naumi** in Bhadon honours the snake saint. **Sanjhi** runs through autumn Navratri. Diwali and Holi are huge, and Holi's second day, **Dulhendi**, has its own Haryana twist: women playfully whip the men of their in-laws' family with twisted cloth ropes called kolda.

Two big fairs are state productions. The **Surajkund International Crafts Mela**, every February in Faridabad, is one of the largest crafts fairs in the world. The **International Gita Mahotsav** in Kurukshetra, held around Gita Jayanti in November-December, has grown into a weeks-long event. In summer, Pinjore holds a Mango Mela in its Mughal garden, a fixture for over 30 years.

spotlights.name: Haryali Teej
spotlights.spot_it: Women in green and red on rope swings hung from neem and peepal trees, singing in groups.
spotlights.story_md: Teej marks the first green after summer. Women, especially new brides who come back to their parents' home for the month of Sawan, hang swings from trees and sing teej songs. Parents send the daughter a **kothli**, a gift bundle of clothes, sweets like ghewar and suhali, and bangles. Hands are decorated with mehndi. In Haryana, Haryali Teej is a state holiday, and the swing (jhoola) is the festival's symbol. Rajput miniature paintings of women on swings in the rain show the same festival three centuries ago.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A monsoon festival that keeps married daughters tied to their parents' home.
spotlights.memory_hook: A swing, a kothli and the first rain.

spotlights.name: Surajkund International Crafts Mela
spotlights.spot_it: Fifteen days of mud-plastered village lanes, painted gates, craft stalls and folk troupes in the Aravalli scrub near Delhi.
spotlights.story_md: Haryana Tourism started the mela to give craftspeople a market without middlemen. Each year a partner country and theme states are chosen. The 39th edition, from 31 January to 15 February 2026, had **Egypt** as partner country and Uttar Pradesh and Meghalaya as theme states. The 2015 fair drew about 1.2 million visitors. Artisans sell directly, folk performers from across India and abroad perform, and the grounds now also host a Diwali mela in October.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India's biggest crafts market in one place.
spotlights.memory_hook: Fifteen days in February when India's villages move to Faridabad.

spotlights.name: International Gita Mahotsav
spotlights.spot_it: Thousands of oil lamps on the steps of Brahma Sarovar, a crafts fair on the banks, Gita recitation over loudspeakers.
spotlights.story_md: Gita Jayanti, the day tradition says the Gita was spoken, falls on Shukla Ekadashi of Margashirsha. Kurukshetra has long marked it; since 2016 Haryana has run it as an 'international' festival lasting two to three weeks, with a partner country, seminars, mass recitation of the Gita by thousands of students, and a nightly Maha Aarti on the sarovar. It is part pilgrimage, part trade fair, part state branding of Kurukshetra as the Gita's city.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Haryana's way of putting Kurukshetra on the global map.
spotlights.memory_hook: Eighteen chapters, thousands of voices, one tank of lamps.

sections.title: How people live: village councils, missing girls, wrestling pits
sections.intro_md:
Two-thirds of Haryanvis lived in villages in 2011, and village life still sets the tone: the **chaupal** (village meeting house), the hookah passed around in the evening, the joint family, the importance of clan (gotra) and land.

The hardest fact about Haryana is its daughters. Census 2011 found **879 females per 1,000 males**, the lowest of any state, and a child sex ratio of just **834**, the result of sex-selective abortion after ultrasound spread in the 1980s. The national campaign **Beti Bachao Beti Padhao** was launched at Panipat on 22 January 2015 for that reason. Registered births improved: 923 girls per 1,000 boys in 2025, the best in five years, then slipped to 900 in the first half of 2026. One consequence has been a shortage of brides, with men marrying women from far-off states.

At the same time, Haryana's daughters now win Olympic medals, and women's literacy and workforce numbers keep rising. The state contains both stories.

spotlights.name: Khap panchayats
spotlights.spot_it: Elders in white turbans on charpais, a microphone, hundreds of men seated on the ground: a khap mahapanchayat.
spotlights.story_md: A khap is a council of a clan or a group of villages, mostly among Jats in Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh. Khaps have no legal power but carry real social weight. They have settled land disputes, mobilised farmers, and backed protests from the 2020-21 farm laws agitation to the 2023 wrestlers' protest. They are also notorious for opposing marriages within the same gotra or village, sometimes with violence, and the Supreme Court has called such diktats illegal. Some khaps have since campaigned against female foeticide and dowry.
spotlights.why_it_matters: An informal power that politicians, police and courts must reckon with.
spotlights.memory_hook: No law gives them power, yet every party courts them.

spotlights.name: The akhara
spotlights.spot_it: A square pit of soft red earth mixed with oil and buttermilk, two men grappling in langots at dawn.
spotlights.story_md: Before wrestling moved to mats, Haryana's sport lived in the akhara, a mud pit attached to a temple or village. Pehlwans train from childhood under a guru, live on milk, ghee and almonds, and keep celibate routines. Village dangals (wrestling fairs) offered prizes from a buffalo to a tractor. Many Olympians, including Yogeshwar Dutt and Bajrang Punia, started in such pits. The diet of milk and ghee from Murrah buffaloes is not incidental: it is the link between Haryana's dairy and its medals.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The training ground of India's Olympic wrestlers.
spotlights.memory_hook: Mud, milk and almonds: the recipe for a medal.

sections.title: Sport: India's medal factory
sections.intro_md:
Haryana has about 2% of India's population and an outsized share of its Olympic medals. At Paris 2024 it sent **25 of India's 117 athletes**, the largest state contingent, including all six wrestlers and four of six boxers. Of India's six medals, four were won by Haryana athletes: Manu Bhaker's two bronzes (one with Sarabjot Singh of Ambala), Neeraj Chopra's silver and Aman Sehrawat's bronze. At Tokyo 2020, Chopra's gold, Ravi Dahiya's silver and Bajrang Punia's bronze all came from Haryana.

Why? Explanations include an akhara culture, a diet heavy in milk, the army and police as employers of athletes, rich cash rewards for medallists, and above all imitation: once a village produces a champion, every family wants one. Bhiwani is called 'Mini Cuba' for its boxers. Shahabad Markanda produces women's hockey players. And a farm family in Balali produced the Phogat sisters, whose story became *Dangal*.

data.label: India's medals won by Haryana athletes
data.note: plus Haryana players in the hockey bronze

spotlights.name: Neeraj Chopra
spotlights.spot_it: A long-haired javelin thrower who turns away and raises his arms before the spear even lands.
spotlights.story_md: Chopra grew up in a farming family in Khandra village and took up javelin as an overweight 13-year-old sent to the gym to slim down. On 7 August 2021 in Tokyo he threw 87.58 m to win India's first Olympic gold in athletics. He added world gold in 2023 and Olympic silver in Paris in 2024. On 16 May 2025 in Doha he finally broke 90 m, 90.23 m, and still came second. His javelin from Tokyo is now in the Olympic Museum in Lausanne.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He made athletics, not just cricket, a dream for Indian kids.
spotlights.memory_hook: The chubby boy from Khandra who threw for gold.

spotlights.name: Manu Bhaker
spotlights.spot_it: A young shooter in a cap and blinkers, one arm extended with an air pistol, the other hand in her pocket.
spotlights.story_md: Bhaker tried boxing, tennis, skating and kabaddi before her father bought her a pistol at 14. By 16 she had World Cup gold. At Tokyo 2020 her pistol malfunctioned and she left in tears. In Paris 2024 she won bronze in the 10 m air pistol, India's first Olympic shooting medal by a woman, then a second bronze in the mixed team with Sarabjot Singh, becoming the first Indian to win two medals at one Games since independence. She also finished fourth in a third event.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Proof that a comeback can be faster than a pistol shot.
spotlights.memory_hook: Broken pistol in Tokyo, two medals in Paris.

spotlights.name: Aman Sehrawat
spotlights.spot_it: A slim 57 kg freestyle wrestler who looks too young for the podium he is standing on.
spotlights.story_md: Sehrawat lost both parents as a child and was raised in the Chhatrasal Stadium wrestling hostel in Delhi. In Paris 2024, aged 21, he won bronze and became India's youngest individual Olympic medallist. Before the bronze bout he was 4.6 kg over the limit; his coaches kept him running and in the sauna through the night and he made weight with 100 g to spare. That came days after Vinesh Phogat was disqualified for being 100 g over. In 2026 he won Asian Games gold.
spotlights.why_it_matters: An orphan from Jhajjar who became India's youngest individual Olympic medallist.
spotlights.memory_hook: Lost 4.6 kg in one night to keep a medal.

spotlights.name: The Phogat sisters
spotlights.spot_it: Two sisters in a village dangal against boys, as told in the 2016 film Dangal.
spotlights.story_md: Mahavir Singh Phogat, a village wrestler, trained his daughters Geeta and Babita in a mud pit despite neighbours' scorn. In 2010 Geeta won India's first Commonwealth Games gold in women's wrestling and later became the first Indian woman wrestler to qualify for the Olympics. Their cousin **Vinesh** won three Commonwealth golds, reached the Paris 2024 final, and was disqualified for being 100 g over weight. Weeks later she entered politics and in October 2024 won the Julana seat in Haryana's assembly.
spotlights.why_it_matters: One family changed what Indian parents thought daughters could do.
spotlights.memory_hook: Mhari chhoriyan chhoron se kam hain ke? (Are our girls any less than boys?)

spotlights.name: Bhiwani, 'Mini Cuba'
spotlights.spot_it: A dusty town of boxing clubs, a SAI hostel and gloves hanging in every second gym.
spotlights.story_md: Captain Hawa Singh, an Asian Games champion, set up boxing training at Bhiwani, and coaches like Jagdish Singh built on it at the Bhiwani Boxing Club. The town's boxers dominated Indian teams. In 2008, **Vijender Singh** of Kaluwas, Bhiwani, won bronze at Beijing, India's first Olympic boxing medal, and several of his teammates were from the same club. Boxing became a route to government jobs and fame. The nickname comes from Cuba, the small island that rules Olympic boxing.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A small town that made India a boxing nation.
spotlights.memory_hook: Mini Cuba: one town, one Olympic first.

spotlights.name: Rani Rampal
spotlights.spot_it: A small, quick forward in India's blue, former captain of the women's hockey team.
spotlights.story_md: Rani's father pulled a horse cart for a living in Shahabad Markanda. She started hockey at 6 at the town's academy under coach Baldev Singh, who has turned Shahabad into a nursery for India's women's team. At 15 she was the youngest player at the 2010 World Cup. As captain, she led India to fourth place at Tokyo 2020, its best Olympic finish in women's hockey. She played 212 internationals and scored 134 goals, and received the Padma Shri in 2020.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She carried women's hockey from a small town to an Olympic semi-final.
spotlights.memory_hook: A cart-puller's daughter who captained India.

sections.title: People to know
sections.intro_md:
Beyond the soldiers and athletes, Haryana has produced people who changed fields far from home.

There is an astronaut from Karnal, a foreign minister from Ambala Cantonment and a steel magnate from a Hisar village, each of whom started in a small town and was told to aim lower. Add to them the names already met today: Hemu, Chhotu Ram, Devi Lal, Lakhmi Chand, Pandit Jasraj, Neeraj Chopra and the Phogats.

Other names worth knowing: the film director and actor **Satish Kaushik** (born in Mahendragarh), actor **Randeep Hooda** (Rohtak), the media founder **Subhash Chandra** of Zee (Hisar), the badminton champion **Saina Nehwal** (born in Hisar), and the cricketer **Kapil Dev**, India's 1983 World Cup captain, who played for Haryana in domestic cricket. Haryana's Ranji team won its only title in 1991 under him.

spotlights.name: Kalpana Chawla
spotlights.spot_it: A short-haired woman in an orange NASA suit, smiling, her name on Karnal's roundabouts, colleges and a medical college.
spotlights.story_md: Chawla grew up in Karnal, decided at 12 to become an aerospace engineer, and fought her father to study engineering in Chandigarh. She moved to the US, earned a PhD, and in 1997 became the first woman of Indian origin in space on shuttle Columbia. On 1 February 2003, returning from her second flight, Columbia broke up over Texas, killing all seven aboard. Haryana named its medical college in Karnal after her.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She made space a career a Karnal girl could imagine.
spotlights.memory_hook: From Karnal's rooftops to orbit, twice.

spotlights.name: Sushma Swaraj
spotlights.spot_it: A woman in a sari with a large red bindi and a sleeveless jacket, answering citizens on Twitter.
spotlights.story_md: Born in Ambala Cantt, Sushma Swaraj became a Haryana cabinet minister in 1977 at 25, then the youngest in the state's history. She went on to be Delhi's first woman chief minister (briefly, in 1998) and India's External Affairs Minister from 2014 to 2019, only the second person after Nehru to complete a full term in that office. She became famous for answering Indians stranded abroad on Twitter, often within hours, and arranging help.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A Haryana minister at 25 who became India's most accessible foreign minister.
spotlights.memory_hook: A tweet to Sushma could get you home.

spotlights.name: O. P. Jindal
spotlights.spot_it: A villager in a white kurta who started a bucket factory and ended with a steel empire.
spotlights.story_md: Om Prakash Jindal was born in Nalwa village and started small, making pipe fittings and buckets in a shed. In 1970 he set up Jindal Strips in Hisar, which grew into the steel and power group now run by his sons as JSW, Jindal Steel and Jindal Stainless. He also entered politics and was Haryana's power minister when he died in a helicopter crash in 2005. His family made Hisar, a dusty market town, an industrial city.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Haryana's best-known self-made industrialist.
spotlights.memory_hook: From buckets in a shed to steel empires.

sections.title: Places to go
sections.intro_md:
Haryana is often driven through rather than visited, which means its sights are uncrowded. A good circuit takes three or four days.

In the north, **Pinjore**'s Mughal garden and the Morni Hills are under an hour from Chandigarh. Along NH-44 you pass Kurukshetra (Brahma Sarovar, Jyotisar, Sheikh Chilli's tomb, a fine Mahabharata-themed panorama), Karnal and Panipat, where a museum and the Kala Amb memorial tell the battle story. In the west, **Hisar** has Firoz Shah's palace and the stub of an Ashokan pillar, and **Rakhigarhi** is a short drive away. In the south, **Narnaul** has Mughal-era buildings including the Jal Mahal and Birbal's Chhatta, and Faridabad has the ancient **Surajkund** reservoir.

Haryana Tourism pioneered highway tourism in the 1970s, building motels named after birds (Magpie, Skylark, Blue Jay) at regular intervals on the highways. Several still operate.

spotlights.name: Pinjore (Yadavindra) Gardens
spotlights.spot_it: Seven descending terraces of lawns, fountains and water channels, with Rajasthani-Mughal pavilions.
spotlights.story_md: The garden was laid out by Fidai Khan, Aurangzeb's foster brother, in the 17th century. Legend says the local hill people told him the place was haunted by goblins and he fled; the garden was neglected until the Patiala rulers restored it and named it after Maharaja Yadavindra Singh. Its seven terraces step down the slope with the Sheesh Mahal, Rang Mahal and Jal Mahal pavilions. The fountains run on evenings and holidays. Every summer it hosts the Pinjore Mango Mela.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Haryana's finest Mughal garden, and still a living one.
spotlights.memory_hook: Seven terraces, a scared Mughal noble and a mango fair.

spotlights.name: Firoz Shah's palace, Hisar
spotlights.spot_it: Rubble-stone walls, an underground palace level, a mosque and a lone pillar standing inside a busy city.
spotlights.story_md: Firoz Shah Tughlaq founded Hisar-e-Firoza, 'Firoz's fort', in 1354 and dug canals from the Yamuna to supply it. Inside the complex are his palace with an underground floor, the Lat ki Masjid, and a pillar assembled from parts of an Ashokan column. Like the Topra pillar, it shows Firoz's habit of collecting older monuments. Historians debate how much of the fort reused earlier buildings and how empty the land was before him; the site is older than its founder's chronicle suggests.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The founding monument of Haryana's fourth-largest city.
spotlights.memory_hook: A sultan's palace with a basement and a borrowed pillar.

spotlights.name: Jal Mahal, Narnaul
spotlights.spot_it: A small domed pavilion with chhatris on a platform in the middle of a large tank, reached by a causeway.
spotlights.story_md: Shah Quli Khan, Akbar's governor of Narnaul, built this water palace in 1591 in the middle of a big tank. In the monsoon the tank filled and the pavilion seemed to float. Today the tank is usually dry, which tells its own story about groundwater in southern Haryana. Narnaul also has Birbal's Chhatta, a multi-storey mansion linked by legend to Akbar's witty minister, and the tomb of Ibrahim Khan Sur, Sher Shah's grandfather.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Mughal Narnaul is one of Haryana's least visited treasures.
spotlights.memory_hook: A floating palace in a lake that has gone dry.

sections.title: How Haryana earns
sections.intro_md:
Haryana's economy rests on three legs. The first is **farming**. The Green Revolution of the late 1960s, built on canals, tube wells, high-yield wheat and rice, and research at the agricultural university in Hisar, turned Haryana into the second-largest contributor of grain to the national stock after Punjab. Haryana also grows a large share of India's **basmati**: with Punjab it supplies about 80% of basmati exports, by one industry estimate.

The second is **industry**, mostly in the NCR belt: cars and two-wheelers in Gurugram, Manesar and Dharuhera; engineering in Faridabad; textiles in Panipat; plywood in Yamunanagar; steel in Hisar; and the Indian Oil refinery at Panipat.

The third is **services**, above all Gurugram's offices. In 2025-26 the state's economy was estimated at **₹13.68 lakh crore**, growing 9.5% in real terms. The costs show up as groundwater depletion, Delhi's winter smog and a deep gap between the NCR and the rest of the state.

spotlights.name: Gurugram's Cyber City
spotlights.spot_it: Glass towers beside the Delhi-Jaipur highway, with an elevated private metro looping between them.
spotlights.story_md: In 1981 Gurgaon was a dusty town of farms. Real-estate firm DLF bought farmland from villagers, then GE set up its back-office operation (later Genpact) here in the late 1990s, and the boom began. Today the city hosts offices of more than 250 Fortune 500 companies and attracts most of Haryana's investment. It was renamed Gurugram in 2016. It also floods in almost every heavy monsoon, because much of it was built over natural drains and lakes faster than public infrastructure could follow.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The engine of Haryana's income, and a warning about unplanned growth.
spotlights.memory_hook: Farmland to Fortune 500 in thirty years, and still flooding.

spotlights.name: The Maruti 800
spotlights.spot_it: A tiny, boxy hatchback, usually white, that every middle-class Indian family of the 1990s seems to remember.
spotlights.story_md: On 14 December 1983, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi handed the keys of the first Maruti 800 to Harpal Singh, an Indian Airlines employee, at the new factory in Gurgaon. The car, built with Suzuki, was cheap, light and reliable, and it ended the era of the Ambassador and Fiat. About 2.87 million were built in 31 years. The Gurugram plant pulled suppliers into the region, and Haryana became the heart of India's car industry, with Maruti adding plants at Manesar and, more recently, Kharkhoda.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The car that put India on wheels was born in Gurugram.
spotlights.memory_hook: Indira's keys, Harpal's car, India's road trip.

spotlights.name: Panipat's textile recycling
spotlights.spot_it: Mountains of sorted old sweaters and jackets in warehouses, shredders, and spinning mills turning out cheap blankets.
spotlights.story_md: Panipat was the 'city of weavers' for durries and handloom. Then it became, by many accounts, the world's largest recycler of woollen clothes. Used garments from Europe and North America arrive, are sorted by colour, shredded into fibre and spun into 'shoddy' yarn for low-cost blankets, many used in disaster relief. Estimates of the volume vary widely, from 100,000 to over 500,000 tonnes a year. The industry employs thousands, but bleaching and dye units have polluted groundwater and drains around the city.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Circular fashion's hidden capital, with real costs.
spotlights.memory_hook: Your old sweater may become a relief blanket in Panipat.

spotlights.name: Stubble burning

where.label: Paddy belt: Karnal, Kaithal, Kurukshetra, Fatehabad

spotlights.spot_it: Orange fire dots across satellite images of Punjab and Haryana each autumn, and smoke drifting toward Delhi.
spotlights.story_md: After the rice harvest, farmers have two or three weeks to sow wheat. Burning the leftover straw is the cheapest way to clear fields, and the smoke adds to Delhi's winter smog. Fines, subsidised machines and payments for not burning have cut fires sharply. The official count for Haryana in the 2025 season was **662**, about 53% lower than in 2024. Critics point out that some farmers now burn after satellite passes, so counts may understate the problem.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A farm decision that shapes the air of 30 million people.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two weeks between harvests, and the whole north holds its breath.

sections.title: What is happening now (2025 to 2026)
sections.intro_md:
Haryana is in the third straight term of a BJP government. **Nayab Singh Saini** became chief minister in March 2024 and won a full term in the October 2024 election. Some of the main threads since:

- **April 2025:** Hisar's Maharaja Agrasen airport started commercial flights, with the first flight to Ayodhya.
- **May 2025:** Neeraj Chopra threw 90.23 m in Doha, his first 90 m throw.
- **25 September 2025:** the **Deen Dayal Lado Lakshmi Yojana** began paying ₹2,100 a month to women in poorer families; in September 2026 the income limit was raised from ₹1 lakh to ₹1.8 lakh.
- **22 December 2025:** **Hansi** became the 23rd district.
- **February 2026:** the 39th Surajkund Mela, with Egypt as partner.
- **May 2026:** the BJP swept municipal elections.
- **June 2026:** Rakhigarhi skeletons were handed to the Anthropological Survey for DNA and isotope work.
- **17 July 2026:** India's first hydrogen train began running between Jind and Sonipat.
- **2026:** the sex ratio at birth fell back to 900 in the first half of the year, after 923 in 2025.

spotlights.spot_it: A soft-spoken chief minister in a white kurta and saffron stole, often at a microphone in Panchkula.
spotlights.story_md: Saini, from an OBC farming family in Ambala district, started as an office assistant in the BJP and rose through the party. He replaced Manohar Lal Khattar as chief minister in March 2024, months before an election many expected the BJP to lose after the farm protests and wrestlers' agitation. Instead the party won 48 of 90 seats in October 2024, its best result in Haryana. His government's flagship is the Lado Lakshmi cash transfer for women.

spotlights.name: India's first hydrogen train
spotlights.spot_it: A 10-coach train with two driving power cars, running 89 km between Jind and Sonipat with only water vapour from its exhaust.
spotlights.story_md: The train was converted from a diesel-electric multiple unit at the Integral Coach Factory. Two power cars each carry fuel cells that combine hydrogen and oxygen to make electricity; the only exhaust is water. Its operating speed is 75 km/h, design speed 110 km/h. A plant at Jind produces about 420 to 430 kg of hydrogen a day by electrolysis and stores up to 3,000 kg. The train makes two round trips a day. Reports of its capacity and power output vary between sources.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A test of whether hydrogen can replace diesel on India's unelectrified lines.

sections.title: Myths and facts
sections.intro_md:
A few things people say about Haryana, tested.

**'Haryana has no culture, only agriculture.'** An old joke, often told by Haryanvis themselves. It ignores saang, ragini, Lakhmi Chand, Pandit Jasraj, Sanjhi, phulkari and some of India's oldest archaeological sites. The joke is a myth.

**'Haryana means abode of God (Hari + ayana).'** A popular etymology, not settled. Other proposals derive it from 'harit aranya' (green forest) or from the Abhira people. Treat it as one theory.

**'Gurugram was the village Dronacharya received from the Pandavas.'** This is the reason given for the 2016 renaming and is local tradition; there is no historical evidence either way.

**'Kurukshetra is where the Mahabharata war happened.'** It is where Hindu tradition sets it, and the area has been sacred for very long. Archaeology has not confirmed a war.

**'Haryana's sex ratio problem is solved.'** No. Births improved after 2015 but fell again to 900 girls per 1,000 boys in early 2026.

sections.title: Recap: Haryana in ten lines
sections.intro_md:
1. A corridor between desert and mountains, so armies passed through it: Tarain, Panipat three times, Karnal.
2. Born 1 November 1966 from Punjab; shares Chandigarh; 23 districts since December 2025.
3. About 2% of India's people, close to 4% of its output; per capita income about 1.75 times India's.
4. Harappan cities like Rakhigarhi, where 2019 DNA showed no steppe ancestry in one woman.
5. Kurukshetra and Jyotisar, the setting of the Gita; Pehowa's priests keep family registers.
6. Hemu nearly stopped Akbar; Banda Singh Bahadur's Lohgarh was the first Sikh capital.
7. Saang, ragini and Lakhmi Chand; Pandit Jasraj has an asteroid.
8. Milk and curd: 1,105 g of milk per person per day, Murrah buffaloes, Murthal parathas, Gohana jalebis.
9. India's medal factory: four of six Paris 2024 medals.
10. Hard truths: the worst sex ratio among states in 2011, stubble smoke, groundwater, and the unbuilt SYL canal.

best_facts.fact: In 1356 Firoz Shah Tughlaq wrapped an Ashokan pillar from Topra in silk, put it on a 42-wheeled cart and a fleet of boats, and re-erected it in Delhi. Its inscriptions later helped James Prinsep decipher Brahmi.
best_facts.why_surprising: A 3rd century BCE monument took a river trip and then unlocked India's oldest script.

best_facts.fact: Of India's six medals at Paris 2024, four were won by athletes from a state with about 2% of the country's people.
best_facts.why_surprising: Haryana's medal share is roughly ten times its population share.

best_facts.fact: Of 61 Harappan skeletons from Rakhigarhi tested in the 2019 study, only one, a woman buried about 4,600 years ago, yielded usable DNA.
best_facts.why_surprising: A whole debate about Indian ancestry rests partly on one person.

best_facts.fact: Haryana makes 1,105 g of milk per person per day, more than double India's average of 471 g.
best_facts.why_surprising: A small dry state is one of India's dairy superpowers.

best_facts.fact: The phrase 'Aaya Ram, Gaya Ram' comes from a Haryana MLA, Gaya Lal, who switched party three times in two weeks in 1967.
best_facts.why_surprising: An everyday Hindi idiom has a real person behind it.

best_facts.fact: Hemu had nearly won the Second Battle of Panipat when an arrow hit his eye; his army fled and Akbar's reign began.
best_facts.why_surprising: One stray arrow decided whether there would be an Akbar.

best_facts.fact: In Marathi, 'Panipat zhala' (a Panipat happened) means a catastrophe, because of the Maratha defeat there in 1761.
best_facts.why_surprising: A Haryana town became a word for disaster in another language.

best_facts.fact: Aman Sehrawat lost 4.6 kg in one night to make weight for his Paris 2024 bronze bout, days after Vinesh Phogat was disqualified for being 100 g over.
best_facts.why_surprising: Olympic medals in Haryana have been won and lost by grams.

best_facts.fact: Census 2011 found Haryana's child sex ratio at 834 girls per 1,000 boys, the lowest of any state, which is why Beti Bachao Beti Padhao was launched in Panipat.
best_facts.why_surprising: A national campaign began where the problem was worst.

best_facts.fact: Pandit Jasraj, born in a village near Hisar, has a minor planet named after him: 300128 Panditjasraj.
best_facts.why_surprising: A Haryana village voice is literally in orbit.

best_facts.fact: Haryana's legislature meets in Chandigarh, a city that belongs to neither Haryana nor Punjab but to the Union.
best_facts.why_surprising: A state capital that is not in the state.

best_facts.fact: At Pehowa, priests can show a visitor the signatures of his grandfathers and great-grandfathers in handwritten registers kept by clan and village.
best_facts.why_surprising: A living paper archive of north Indian families.

best_facts.fact: The first Maruti 800 was handed over at Gurgaon on 14 December 1983 by Indira Gandhi to Harpal Singh; about 2.87 million were built.
best_facts.why_surprising: India's car revolution began in a Haryana factory.

best_facts.fact: India's first hydrogen train began running in July 2026 between Jind and Sonipat; its only exhaust is water.
best_facts.why_surprising: Clean rail's Indian debut was on a quiet Haryana branch line.

best_facts.fact: Sultanpur National Park covers only 1.43 km² yet draws Siberian and Central Asian birds every winter, 15 km from Gurugram's towers.
best_facts.why_surprising: A postage-stamp wetland is an international bird stop.

best_facts.fact: Banda Singh Bahadur's Lohgarh, in Haryana's Shivalik forest, was the capital of the first Sikh state (1710 to 1716).
best_facts.why_surprising: The first Sikh state was not in Punjab proper.

best_facts.why_surprising: A sweet usually eaten in handfuls is sold by the piece like a cake.

side_dish.title: The Green Revolution: why short wheat changed Haryana
side_dish.body_md:
Before the 1960s, Haryana's wheat was tall. Feed it more fertiliser and it grew taller still, until the heavy heads bent the stems and the crop collapsed in the wind. Farmers call this lodging. More fertiliser meant more lost grain.

The fix came from Japan and Mexico. A Japanese variety, Norin 10, carried genes that kept the stem short. Norman Borlaug's team in Mexico crossed it into wheats that also resisted rust disease. The result: dwarf plants that put their energy into grain instead of straw, and could carry two or three times the fertiliser without falling over.

India imported these seeds in the mid-1960s, after two failed monsoons and food aid from the US. Haryana was ready for them: it had the Western Yamuna and Bhakra canals, it was digging tube wells, and from 1970 it had an agricultural university in Hisar adapting the seeds. Wheat yields roughly tripled in two decades. Rice followed, and Haryana became a grain exporter to the rest of India.

The bill came later. Rice, a water-hungry crop in a dry state, drained the aquifers; many blocks in Haryana now pump more than the rain refills. The short gap between rice harvest and wheat sowing created the stubble fires. The science that ended famine also built the state's biggest environmental problems. Both are true at once.

offline_task.title: Make Haryanvi kadhi pakora tonight
offline_task.body_md:
**Serves 3. 40 minutes. Use curd that is a day or two old and slightly sour.**

**For the kadhi**
- 1 cup sour curd, 3 tablespoons besan (gram flour), 3 cups water
- Half a teaspoon turmeric, salt
- Tempering: 1 tablespoon ghee, 1 teaspoon cumin, half a teaspoon fenugreek seeds, 2 dried red chillies, a pinch of hing

**For the pakoras**
- Half a cup besan, 1 onion finely sliced, 1 green chilli, a pinch of ajwain, salt, water to make a thick batter, oil for frying

**Steps**
1. Whisk curd, besan, turmeric and water until there are no lumps.
2. Bring to a boil on medium heat, stirring all the time so it does not split. Then simmer on low for 25 minutes, stirring now and then. It should coat a spoon thinly.
3. Meanwhile, drop spoonfuls of pakora batter into hot oil and fry until golden.
4. Add the pakoras and salt to the kadhi and simmer 5 more minutes.
5. Heat ghee, add cumin, fenugreek, chillies and hing, and pour it sizzling over the kadhi.

Eat with rice or roti. Notice how sour, thin and savoury it is next to a sweet Gujarati kadhi: that is the taste of a dairy state using up its curd.
